{
  "analysis": "The training data reveals that German legal texts frequently use academic and professional titles (Mag., Dr., Univ.-Prof., etc.) immediately preceding person names, often with suffixes like LL.M. or Bakk. iur. The primary failure mode in generic NER is missing these titles or capturing them as part of the entity when they are not, or conversely, missing the name if the title is complex. The rules must specifically target the pattern of Title + Name + (Optional Suffix) to ensure high precision in this domain.",
  "strategy": "Create a set of regex rules that specifically target German legal titles (Mag., Dr., Univ.-Prof., etc.) followed by capitalized names and optional academic suffixes, using context anchors like 'durch den Richter' or 'in der Beschwerdesache' to disambiguate.",
  "note": "Every rule includes output_template and output_key. Patterns use capture groups for the name part to ensure correct span extraction if titles vary, but full match is used for simplicity where the title is part of the entity definition in this context.",
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "legal_titles_with_names",
      "description": "Matches person entities preceded by common German legal/academic titles (Mag., Dr., Univ.-Prof., Priv.-Doz., etc.) followed by a name and optional suffixes.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Mag\\.?|Dr\\.?|Univ\\.-Prof\\.?|Priv\\.-Doz\\.?|Hon\\.-Prof\\.?|OMedR|KommR|RgR|PhD|LL\\.M\\.?|B\\.A\\.?|B\\.B\\.A\\.?|Bakk\\. iur\\.|Bakk\\. phil\\.|MedR|OSR|Techn R)\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 10,
      "reasoning": "Covers the most frequent pattern in the training data where titles are explicitly attached to names (e.g., 'Mag. Martin Kuprian', 'Univ.-Prof.in Dolores Morhard'). The pattern captures the title and the full name."
    },
    {
      "name": "names_after_prepositions",
      "description": "Matches person names appearing after specific prepositions or verbs common in legal texts (e.g., 'gegen', 'durch', 'von', 'als').",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:gegen|durch|von|als|in der Beschwerdesache)\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 8,
      "reasoning": "Captures names that might not have a title immediately preceding them but are clearly identified by their grammatical role in the sentence (e.g., 'gegen Shoshana Romaike', 'durch den Richter R.' - though 'R.' is tricky, this helps with full names). Note: This rule is less specific than the title rule but catches cases like 'Herrn Ronald Jundt' if 'Herrn' is not in the title list, or simple names after prepositions."
    },
    {
      "name": "names_after_herrn_frau",
      "description": "Matches person names preceded by 'Herrn' or 'Frau' (accusative/dative forms common in legal texts).",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Herrn|Frau)\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "Specifically targets the pattern seen in examples like 'Herrn Ronald Jundt' or 'Frau Ruperta Keymer'. Using a capture group ensures only the name is extracted, not the honorific."
    },
    {
      "name": "names_in_address_context",
      "description": "Matches names that appear immediately before an address pattern (street, number, postal code, city).",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:in der Beschwerdesache)\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)\\s*,\\s*[A-Za-z]+\\s+\\d+",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "Leverages the strong context of an address following a name to identify the person (e.g., 'Shoshana Romaike, Anton-Schwetter-Gasse 6'). This is a very strong anchor in legal documents."
    },
    {
      "name": "single_word_names_in_context",
      "description": "Matches single capitalized words that appear in contexts where a person is likely (e.g., after 'des', 'der', 'den' if not a noun, or in lists).",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:des|der|den)\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+)(?=\\s+(?:von|als|in|auf|mit))",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 4,
      "reasoning": "Catches cases like 'des RgR Willibald Broot' (where Broot is part of a compound title/name) or 'des Herrn Domrose'. This is a fallback for shorter names or specific grammatical structures."
    }
  ],
  "deleted_rules": []
}

- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.
